title: Marketing Research Digest — Consumer Psychology — 2026-11-05

studies.title: One "swap and save" nudge can rewire a shopper's habit for 10 trips
studies.paper_title: Swap and Save: How a Button Shapes Lasting Online Grocery Shopping Behavior
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed behavior in the mineral water category on an online grocery price comparison platform that shows real-time "swap and save" buttons prompting shoppers toward cheaper alternatives. Shoppers who accepted a prompt and switched products were 23.7 percentage points more likely to pick that same alternative on later visits, and the effect persisted for up to about 10 shopping trips. The analysis indicates the stickiness came from product discovery rather than accumulated cost savings.
studies.why_it_matters: It quantifies how a single, cheap interface element can permanently break habitual brand loyalty in a repeat-purchase category, which is both a growth channel for challenger brands and an unglamorous threat to incumbents.
studies.story_angle_primary: Incumbent brands in habitual categories should audit where comparison prompts appear against their SKUs and what they cost in long-run repeat purchase, not just the single lost basket; challengers should treat swap buttons as a trial-generation mechanism whose payoff is discovery, not discount. The effect is measured on one platform and one category, so the magnitude is a benchmark to test, not a universal number.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Much of what looks like brand loyalty in the supermarket may just be inertia: shoppers often repurchase the same bottled water because they have never been shown the alternative, and a single prompt is enough to reset the default for months.
studies.caveats: Single category (mineral water), single price comparison platform, one market; observational platform data rather than a randomized experiment, so switching shoppers may differ from non-switchers; effects measured over a short horizon of roughly 10 trips.
studies.verdict_notes: Core numbers (23.7pp, 10 trips, discovery mechanism) are accurate, but "permanently" and "for months" in the framing overstate a 10-trip horizon the digest's own caveat flags as short.

studies.title: Japanese shoppers trust "made here" far more than they trust awards
studies.paper_title: Quality Signals and Consumer Choice: The Roles of Origin, Awards and Place Attractiveness
studies.the_study: In a discrete choice experiment, 1,040 Japanese consumers made soy sauce choices producing 18,720 alternative-specific observations, testing three quality signals: broad domestic origin, a fine-grained regional origin cue (Soma), and award recognition. Mixed logit models found domestic soybean origin was robustly and consistently preferred over imported origin, while the narrow regional cue was positive but with wide variation across consumers. Award recognition was not a uniformly positive signal; it was associated with choice more positively only among consumers who rated the linked place as attractive.
studies.why_it_matters: Awards and medals are a staple of food and drink packaging, yet this suggests they may do little on their own and can depend entirely on whether the consumer has a positive image of the place behind the product.
studies.story_angle_primary: Food and beverage brands should test whether award badges actually move choice in their category or whether the origin claim is doing all the work, and consider that regional-origin storytelling only pays off where the region already carries positive associations. This is a choice experiment in one country and one product, so treat it as a prompt to run package-cue tests rather than as a verdict on awards everywhere.
studies.story_angle_secondary: That gold medal sticker on a bottle may be persuading you less than you think, and the words "domestically grown" are probably doing the real work on the shelf.
studies.caveats: Hypothetical choice tasks rather than real purchases; single country (Japan) and single category (soy sauce); place attractiveness was measured after the choice tasks and after exposure to a tourism website, so the authors explicitly describe that link as associational, not causal.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, N, observation count and main effects all match; the award moderation is described slightly more absolutely than the abstract's conditional wording.

studies.title: Lonely shoppers aren't just buying more, they're buying impulsively
studies.paper_title: When Loneliness Becomes a Consumer Welfare Risk: Symptom‐Level and Neurocognitive Evidence From Compulsive Buying
studies.the_study: Study 1 surveyed 2,433 university consumers and found that impulsive buying tendency statistically accounted for the link between loneliness and compulsive buying (indirect effect = 0.140), with a stronger association among women; item-level analysis pointed to spontaneous, action-oriented and reckless purchasing rather than planned compensatory spending. Study 2 analyzed resting-state fMRI from 89 participants and found, among men, a tentative pathway from loneliness to compulsive buying via default mode network activity. The authors label the neural pathway exploratory, as component correlations did not survive full correction.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes loneliness-driven overspending as a self-regulation failure at the moment of purchase, which is precisely the state that one-click checkout, limited-time offers and livestream shopping are designed to exploit.
studies.story_angle_primary: Marketers operating in high-impulse formats should expect scrutiny over vulnerable-consumer harm, and consider whether friction-reducing features (saved cards, countdown timers, push alerts) are disproportionately converting people in a dysregulated state. For brands building wellbeing credentials, designing in pause points is a testable differentiator rather than just a compliance exercise.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you shop when you feel isolated, the risk isn't retail therapy itself but speed: the damage shows up in unplanned, reckless purchases rather than in deliberate treat-buying.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey in Study 1, so causation cannot be established; student/university sample; the neuroimaging sample is small (N=89) and the authors state the neural pathway is exploratory and did not survive full-family correction; gender differences are post hoc.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample sizes, indirect effect (0.140), gender patterns and the exploratory status of the neural pathway all match the abstract; caveats are appropriately cautious.

studies.title: Why rival products end up nearly identical: advertising less is a way to compete less
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: Why are products so similar despite diverse consumer needs? The interplay between advertising and horizontal product differentiation
studies.the_study: This analytical modeling paper asks why real firms are far less differentiated than standard price-competition theory predicts. Letting firms endogenously choose product positioning, advertising and price, the authors show that firms can soften price competition by limiting informative or reminder advertising instead of moving apart in product space, allowing them to cluster in the middle of the market. The clustered, low-advertising outcome is especially likely when advertising is expensive, while partial or full differentiation emerges under other cost and preference conditions.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers a competitive logic for a pattern marketers see constantly: me-too products backed by surprisingly restrained advertising, where underspending is a strategic choice rather than timidity.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brand leaders should interrogate whether their category's low ad intensity reflects a tacit equilibrium that collapses the moment someone spends aggressively, and model the price-war risk of ramping up reach in a collocated market. Treat this as a framework for competitive war-gaming, not an empirical finding about any particular category.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The reason competing products feel interchangeable may be less about lazy design than about firms quietly avoiding a fight, since telling more consumers about your differences invites a price war.
studies.caveats: Purely theoretical modeling with no empirical data; conclusions depend on assumptions about travel/disutility cost shape and consumer distribution.
studies.verdict_notes: Faithful summary of an analytical modeling paper, with the theoretical nature and the travel-cost assumption dependence both flagged.

studies.title: Cool colors can excite too — if you use more than one
studies.paper_title: Color me aroused while keeping the cool
studies.journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
studies.the_study: Marketing researchers ran eight experiments (seven preregistered, 1,724 participants total) testing whether logos must be warm or highly saturated to arouse consumers. Using eye tracking, galvanic skin response and pupil dilation in a behavioral lab, plus three studies involving real product choices, they found that multicolor logos built from cool hues (blues, greens) were more physiologically arousing than single cool-color designs. The mechanism was curiosity triggered by visual complexity, and the arousal boost carried through to higher willingness to pay and actual choice.
studies.why_it_matters: It breaks the long-standing design rule that red and orange are the only route to excitement, giving brands in categories that lean cool and calm — tech, finance, health, sustainability — a way to generate energy without abandoning their palette.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brand and design teams revisiting a logo refresh can test multicolor cool variants against a single-hue mark, measuring curiosity and attention rather than just liking. The biometric and real-choice evidence here is unusually strong for a design paper, but it is still lab and study-based: run the variants through live creative tests before committing to a system-wide rebrand.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Your eye is drawn to brand marks that look slightly puzzling. A logo made of several cool colors makes you curious, and curiosity — not warmth or brightness — is what quietly raises how much you are willing to pay.
studies.caveats: Lab experiments and choice tasks rather than market-level sales data; arousal effects measured over short exposures, so durability over time is untested.
studies.verdict_notes: Experiment count, preregistration, N=1,724, biometric measures, real-choice studies, curiosity mechanism and WTP/choice outcomes all match. (Abstract notes only six of the eight experiments appear in the main text, a detail the digest omits without distorting the finding.)

studies.title: Clustering a few bad reviews together makes them feel like the majority
studies.paper_title: The Power of Review Contiguity: How Sequential Viewing Shapes Consumer Judgment
studies.the_study: Across four experiments, researchers tested how the ordering and presentation of online reviews shapes judgment. When reviews were shown one at a time (as in sequential scrolling), bunching a handful of minority reviews into an unbroken run made consumers believe that viewpoint was far more common than it was, shifting product evaluations accordingly; scattering the same reviews among the majority weakened the effect substantially. The pattern held for both negative and positive minority reviews, faded under cognitive load, and was stronger on mobile than desktop.
studies.why_it_matters: Sorting and layout choices that look purely functional — "most recent first," infinite scroll, mobile card stacks — can distort how prevalent a complaint or a rave appears, with real consequences for conversion and for platform fairness.
studies.story_angle_primary: Retail and platform teams should audit review sorting as a persuasion variable, not just a UX detail: test whether interleaving versus clustering dissenting reviews changes conversion and return rates, and ask whether the current default inadvertently amplifies a small minority on mobile. These are controlled experiments, so treat the effect as a hypothesis to A/B test on live traffic.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you hit three bad reviews in a row while scrolling, your brain concludes the product is widely disliked — even when those three are the only critics among dozens. Checking the overall star distribution is a cheap corrective to what the scroll just did to you.
studies.caveats: Experimental studies with constructed review sets rather than real purchase behavior on a live platform; effect sizes in the field are untested.
studies.verdict_notes: All four experiments, the mediator, and all three boundary conditions (cognitive load, mobile vs desktop, positive and negative minorities) are correctly reported; only the magnitude intensifiers go beyond the abstract.

studies.title: Typing beats talking: text AI recommendations get adopted more than voice
studies.paper_title: Talking or typing? How GenAI modality, product type, and multitasking shape recommendation response behaviour
studies.the_study: Five studies, including a preliminary field study using actual customer interactions in a commercial setting plus four controlled experiments in China, compared text-based and voice-based generative AI product recommendations. Text recommendations were adopted more overall, and the gap depended on what was being sold: text won for search products with specifications to compare, while voice performed better for experience products. Processing fluency mediated the effect, and when consumers were multitasking under cognitive load, voice became the stronger format across product types.
studies.why_it_matters: As brands bolt conversational AI onto storefronts and apps, modality is being treated as a technical choice rather than a persuasion variable — and this evidence suggests it materially changes whether shoppers act on advice.
studies.story_angle_primary: Rather than defaulting to a single AI assistant format, test modality by category and context: text for spec-heavy search goods, voice for experiential purchases and for moments when the shopper is driving, cooking or otherwise distracted. The field component gives this more real-world grounding than most GenAI papers, but the experiments were run in one country and need replication in your own market.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Talking to an AI shopping assistant feels modern, but most people find it harder to absorb product details by ear — which is why voice works best when your hands are busy and the thing you are buying is about feel rather than specs.
studies.caveats: Experiments conducted in China, limiting generalizability; four of the five studies were controlled lab or online experiments; the field study's scale and partner are not detailed in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Five studies, the field component, the search/experience moderation, processing fluency mediation and the multitasking reversal are all accurate; the claim that all four experiments ran in China goes slightly beyond the abstract.

studies.title: Eye tracking shows bad brand news wins the attention battle — and specific crises leave specific scars
studies.paper_title: Consumer responses to conflicting brand news in digital feeds
studies.the_study: Three studies traced how negative brand information competes with positive information in digital feeds: within-participant eye tracking (n=117), a randomized experiment combining eye tracking and surveys (n=285), and a three-wave longitudinal experiment (n=279 at the final wave). Negative items drew more visual attention than concurrent positive items, and a larger share of negative attention intensified contempt for worker-treatment violations and disgust for integrity violations, which in turn eroded beliefs about employee care and ethical integrity respectively. Anger and sadness did not mediate the damage, and the hit to the specific legitimacy belief was larger and more persistent than the hit to overall brand evaluation.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests crisis recovery cannot be bought with generic positive messaging: if the accusation is about how you treat workers, only evidence about worker treatment repairs the belief that was actually damaged.
studies.story_angle_primary: Rebuild crisis playbooks around the specific obligation under attack rather than a flood of upbeat brand content, and consider that feed-level attention competition is where the damage starts. Note that these are controlled experiments with student-scale samples, so treat the emotion-specific pathways as a framework for message testing rather than a settled formula.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Scrolling past a brand's good news and bad news in the same feed, your eyes go to the bad news — and the resulting judgment is oddly surgical: you may still think the brand is fine overall while permanently doubting that it treats its staff decently.
studies.caveats: Experimental designs with stimuli rather than live crises; moderate sample sizes; longitudinal horizon limited to three waves.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample sizes and the emotion-specific pathways are reported correctly, but the social identification moderator is dropped, the samples are described as "student-scale" without support, and "permanently" overstates persistence.

studies.title: In livestream selling, chatting with viewers outsells the hard hook
studies.paper_title: Decoding the “emotion-trust” chain: how streamer speech types influence consumer behavior intentions through S-O-R framework
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.the_study: A between-subjects experiment presented 603 participants with real livestreaming video stimuli using one of three streamer speech styles: hook-oriented (attention-grabbing openers), mechanism-oriented (explaining deals and product logic) and interaction-oriented (conversing with viewers). Interaction-oriented speech produced the strongest emotional response, trust and purchase intention, followed by mechanism-oriented, with hook-oriented speech weakest for high-involvement symbolic products. Mediation analysis supported a sequence in which emotion builds trust, which then drives intention.
studies.why_it_matters: Livestream commerce coaching tends to emphasize punchy hooks and urgency, but for considered, identity-relevant purchases the evidence points toward conversational engagement as the more persuasive script.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands running or sponsoring live shopping should test scripted hooks against genuine viewer interaction by product tier, particularly for higher-ticket symbolic items where trust is the bottleneck. This is a scenario-based experiment with stated intentions, so validate against actual conversion data from your own streams before rewriting talent briefs.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The livestream host who answers your comment is doing more to sell you something than the one shouting about a limited-time deal — at least when the product is expensive enough that you need to trust someone first.
studies.caveats: Scenario-based experiment with video stimuli rather than real purchases; outcome is stated behavioral intention, not observed buying; single-country context and a focus on high-involvement symbolic products.
studies.verdict_notes: N=603, three speech conditions, the ranking of effects, the high-involvement symbolic product context and the emotion→trust→intention mediation all match; caveats correctly note stated intention rather than purchases.

studies.title: Lonely shoppers reach for busier packaging
studies.paper_title: The Pursuit of Security: How Loneliness Shapes Consumers' Preference for Simple Versus Complex Packaging Designs
studies.the_study: Across seven studies (one survey plus six experiments, N=1,636 total), researchers tested how loneliness shifts preferences for simple versus complex product packaging. Lonely consumers consistently leaned toward visually complex, densely designed packaging, and the effect ran through what the authors call a desire for "symbolic security" — complex designs appear to feel protective or enveloping. The effect was strongest among people low in a dispositional sense of security and faded among those who already felt secure.
studies.why_it_matters: Minimalism has been the default design orthodoxy for a decade, but this suggests the audience's emotional state, not fashion, may determine which design wins — and loneliness is widespread and measurable at the segment level.
studies.story_angle_primary: Design and packaging teams could test complex versus minimalist variants against audiences segmented by loneliness-adjacent signals (solo households, late-night delivery windows, categories bought for comfort) rather than assuming clean design always converts. These are lab-scale results, so treat them as a hypothesis for a packaging A/B test, not a redesign mandate.
studies.story_angle_secondary: It's a quiet example of how mood leaks into taste: the same box can look cluttered when you feel connected and reassuring when you feel alone. Worth noticing the next time a product's look suddenly appeals.
studies.caveats: Experimental and survey studies rather than observed purchases; loneliness was often manipulated or measured momentarily; packaging preference is a stated response, not real shelf behavior; sample sizes per condition are modest across seven studies.
studies.verdict_notes: Seven studies, N=1,636, the complex-packaging effect and the symbolic security mechanism are accurate; the security-trait moderation is described as the effect "fading" rather than weakening.

studies.title: The more unequal people think their society is, the more they buy self-improvement
studies.paper_title: How Perceived Economic Inequality Shapes Consumers' Preferences for Self‐Improvement Consumption
studies.the_study: Six studies across the United States, Japan and China (N=2,626) tested whether perceptions of economic inequality drive demand for self-improvement products and services — courses, skills training, personal development. Participants primed with or perceiving high inequality consistently preferred self-improvement options over comparable non-self-improvement ones, with the effect running through heightened status ambition. Notably, status anxiety, loss of control, negative mood and envy were all tested as alternative mechanisms and none held up; the effect also extended to purchase intention and recommendation likelihood.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes the self-improvement boom as a response to perceived reward gaps rather than to fear or anxiety, which changes how such products should be positioned and where demand should be expected to grow.
studies.story_angle_primary: For education, fitness, coaching and skills brands, the finding suggests aspiration-and-reward messaging ('the gap between levels is big, and you can climb') may outperform anxiety-based framing. Test geographic or temporal targeting against inequality perception data — but remember these were controlled experiments, not market-level sales evidence.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The impulse to self-optimize may be less about personal insecurity than about reading the scoreboard: when the top looks far above the middle, striving feels worth it. That's a useful thing to notice about your own buying of courses and gear.
studies.caveats: Experiments with hypothetical choices and stated intentions rather than real purchases; perceived inequality was often manipulated; the predicted moderation by perceived social mobility did not appear; three countries but all via experimental samples.
studies.verdict_notes: Study count, countries, N, mediator and null alternative mechanisms all match; headline converts preference/intention into purchase behavior.

studies.title: "Buy experiences, not things" only works if you want them for the right reasons
studies.paper_title: When ‘Buy Experiences, Not Stuff’ Backfires: Why Life Goals and Motivation Matter
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 1,409 adults (1,324 retained) across Western societies (UK, US) and East Asian societies (Hong Kong, Macao, mainland China, South Korea, Taiwan), testing whether people's life goals predict *why* they buy experiences and what that does to psychological well-being. The negative route held everywhere: people with extrinsic life goals (status, image, money) pursued experiences out of pressure or self-image concerns, and that controlled motivation was linked to frustration of basic psychological needs. The positive route was weaker — intrinsic goals predicted autonomous motivation in both samples, but that motivation only translated into need satisfaction among Western respondents, not East Asian ones.
studies.why_it_matters: The "experiences make you happier than stuff" claim underpins a decade of travel, events and hospitality marketing, and this evidence suggests the benefit is conditional — and that the harmful pathway may be the more reliable one.
studies.story_angle_primary: Experience marketers lean heavily on well-being promises; this is a signal to test whether status-coded framing ("the trip everyone will envy," shareable moments) attracts customers for motives that leave them worse off and less likely to return. Worth probing whether intrinsically framed messaging — curiosity, connection, skill — produces different post-purchase satisfaction, particularly in East Asian markets where the well-being payoff did not appear.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Booking a concert or a holiday is not automatically better for you than buying a sofa. What seems to matter is whether you genuinely want the experience or feel you ought to have it — for the photos, the story, the sense of keeping up.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey, so no causal claims; self-reported motivations and well-being rather than observed spending; "Western" and "East Asian" groupings flatten considerable within-region variation.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample (1,409 collected, 1,324 retained), country groupings, and the asymmetry between the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways are reported correctly; caveats flag the cross-sectional design.

studies.title: Sustainability labels moved shoppers on flour — and did nothing for shoes
studies.paper_title: From Forest to Market: Sustainability Signals and Consumer Decision-Making for Amazonian Products
studies.the_study: In an online survey experiment with 991 Brazilian consumers, researchers tested three ways of signaling sustainability on Amazon rainforest products: a conventional environmental label, a "co-creation" label highlighting collaboration with local forest communities, and a traceability QR code showing product origin. For manioc flour, all three cues raised perceived sustainability — the environmental label most strongly — and that in turn raised purchase intention. For shoes, none of the cues had any effect on either perceived sustainability or intention to buy, and consumers' prior knowledge of sustainability labels and personal green values did not change the outcomes.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests sustainability cues are not a portable credibility device: they land where consumers already expect an origin story (food) and evaporate in categories where they do not, which should change how brands budget certification and traceability spend by category.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before paying for certification or building QR traceability, test whether the cue actually shifts perception in your specific category — and note that the socially framed "made with local communities" claim underperformed the plain environmental label, suggesting social-value claims may need far clearer communication to register at all.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shoppers read eco-claims very selectively. The same reassurance that makes you trust a bag of flour may not even be noticed on a pair of shoes — which means a label's presence tells you less about a product's impact than about which aisle it is sitting in.
studies.caveats: Online survey experiment measuring stated purchase intention, not real purchases; single country (Brazil) and only two product categories; cues were presented in isolation rather than on a crowded shelf.
studies.verdict_notes: N=991 Brazilian online survey experiment, three cues, two categories, strongest effect for the environmental/sustainability label, null results for shoes and null moderation by knowledge and values all match the abstract; caveats correctly note intention rather than purchase.

studies.title: Business schools say AACSB accreditation puts them in the top 5% — in the US it's more like half
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: AACSB Accreditation Claims by U.S. Business Schools: An Ethical Perspective
studies.the_study: The authors conducted a large-scale census of US institutions with a school or division of business and compared the results with the marketing claim, widely repeated on school websites, that only 5–6% of business schools worldwide hold AACSB accreditation. While the global figure may be accurate, roughly 52% of US institutions with a business school are AACSB accredited — meaning the accreditation does not signal "elite" status to the American students who actually use it to choose a college. The paper assesses the claim against FTC, Better Business Bureau, Institute for Advertising Ethics and International Chamber of Commerce standards on misleading or materially incomplete marketing communications.
studies.why_it_matters: It is a documented case of a technically true statistic becoming misleading when aimed at a domestic audience — and it comes from the very institutions that teach marketing ethics.
studies.story_angle_primary: A clean cautionary example of denominator framing: any brand quoting a scarcity statistic should ask whether the population in the claim matches the population making the decision, because regulators judge claims by what the audience reasonably infers, not by what is literally defensible.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families comparing colleges, AACSB accreditation is a floor rather than a distinction in the US — a reminder to check what a credential's "top X%" claim is actually a percentage of.
studies.caveats: US-only; descriptive and normative rather than an experiment — it does not measure whether the claim actually changed any student's choice.
studies.verdict_notes: The ~52% US figure, the 5–6% global claim, the four cited ethics codes, and the descriptive/normative nature of the paper are all consistent with the abstract.

studies.title: Body-positive ads land with women — and backfire with men
studies.paper_title: Differences in men’s and women’s responses to large-size versus idealized advertising models
studies.the_study: Researchers tested how men and women respond to ads featuring sex-matched large-size models versus idealized ones (thin models for women, muscular models for men), measuring attitudes toward the ad and the brand plus the emotions driving them. Women rated ads and brands more favorably when the model was large-size rather than idealized thin, and positive emotions explained the lift. Men went the other way: large-size male models produced less favorable ad and brand attitudes than muscular models, with negative emotions doing the mediating work.
studies.why_it_matters: Body-inclusive casting has become a default signal of brand virtue, but this evidence suggests the payoff is gendered — what reads as empowering to a female audience may read as off-putting to a male one.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands running inclusive-casting campaigns should test creative separately by target gender rather than assuming a single body-positive execution travels across audiences; the asymmetry here is a hypothesis worth validating with real campaign data before rolling inclusive casting into menswear, fitness or grooming lines.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Body positivity in advertising has largely been a conversation about women. This research hints that men's ideals around muscularity remain comparatively untouched — and that audiences may react to ad bodies with emotion first, judgment second.
studies.caveats: Experimental ad exposure measuring attitudes rather than purchases; the abstract does not report sample size, composition or country, and the model manipulations were limited to thin-versus-large for women and muscular-versus-large for men.
studies.verdict_notes: Direction of both effects and the distinct positive/negative emotion mediators match; the digest correctly flags that the abstract reports no sample size, composition or country.

studies.title: People who check receipts, not memory, weather financial shocks better
studies.paper_title: Tracking Every Dollar: How Do Information Sources Support Budgeting?
studies.the_study: Using nationally representative US data from the 2023 Survey and Diary of Consumer Payment Choice, researchers examined how people actually reconstruct their spending when tracking expenses. Sixty-five percent drew on several information sources at once, and using more sources — particularly financial records and receipts rather than memory — produced fewer imprecise and incomplete expense records. Greater precision in recorded amounts was in turn associated with stronger household financial resilience, including the ability to absorb an emergency expense and avoid cash-flow-related fees.
studies.why_it_matters: Budgeting advice usually focuses on whether people budget at all; this suggests the mechanics of how they capture the numbers may be what separates effective budgeting from the illusion of it.
studies.story_angle_primary: For banks, fintechs and payment apps, the finding points to a product opportunity: features that automatically consolidate receipts, statements and transaction feeds into a single record may matter more to customer financial health than yet another budgeting template or nudge.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you budget from memory, you are probably budgeting wrong. The households that could cover an emergency bill were the ones whose expense records were precise — and precision came from paperwork and digital records, not recall.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey and diary data, so associations between tracking quality and financial resilience cannot establish causation (resilient households may simply keep better records); single country (US).
studies.verdict_notes: Data source, 65% figure and the two associations are reported correctly, but the body uses a causal verb and the headline chains two separate associations.

studies.title: Instagram commenters are running their own forensic audits of AI influencers
studies.paper_title: Crowd Forensics and Warrant Braiding: Collaborative Persuasion Knowledge in AI Influencer Threads
studies.the_study: Two independent coders analyzed 1,613 organic comments on 128 Instagram posts from 12 global synthetic (AI) influencer accounts spanning 2018 to 2025. Commenters routinely turned threads into collective investigations — inspecting glitches, lighting and content provenance to challenge the post's legitimacy — a pattern the authors call "crowd forensics," present in 100 of the 128 threads and more common on posts carrying AI disclosure. A counter-pattern, "warrant braiding," in which commenters assembled aesthetic, technological and normative justifications that make synthetic engagement feel acceptable, appeared in just 32 threads and clustered on carousels and lower-visibility posts.
studies.why_it_matters: Persuasion knowledge is no longer a private judgment formed in one consumer's head — audiences build and inherit suspicion collectively in comment sections, meaning one skeptical commenter can shape how everyone who scrolls past reads the ad.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands deploying synthetic influencers should treat the comment section as part of the creative: AI disclosure appears to invite more scrutiny rather than defuse it, and format choices (carousels, lower-visibility posts) correlate with more accepting discourse — both worth testing deliberately rather than discovering after launch.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The next time you spot an uncanny hand or odd lighting in an influencer post, someone has probably already said so in the comments. Audiences are crowdsourcing their own authenticity checks, and the verdict is usually skeptical.
studies.caveats: Observational content analysis of public comments on a single platform (Instagram) and 12 accounts — it documents discourse, not the effect of that discourse on attitudes or purchases; comment sections are also shaped by moderation and are not representative of all viewers.
studies.verdict_notes: Comment count, post count, accounts, date range, double coding, and the 100/128 vs 32 thread split with their respective conditions all match; caveats correctly frame it as content analysis of discourse.

studies.title: Shoppers let their guard down with AI influencers — but only on low-stakes buys
studies.paper_title: The algorithmic mirror: AI disinhibition and anxiety-driven compensatory consumption
studies.the_study: Across four experiments, participants were shown human influencers, photorealistic AI influencers or animated AI influencers promoting products at varying levels of risk, and researchers traced how appearance anxiety translated into buying. Anxiety increased fear of missing out, which drove compensatory buying regardless of influencer type. But in AI conditions an additional direct route to impulsive and compulsive buying appeared — stronger for animated than realistic avatars — which the authors attribute to the absence of social evaluation; the effect faded as product risk rose and vanished for high-risk categories.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests virtual influencers may lower consumers' self-regulatory brakes precisely because nobody feels judged by a cartoon — an effectiveness advantage in fashion and beauty that doubles as a consumer-protection concern.
studies.story_angle_primary: Marketers weighing AI influencers should note the category boundary this research implies: low-risk, identity-expressive goods look like the sweet spot, while health and financial products appear to trigger scrutiny that neutralizes the effect. The ethical flip side — that the mechanism works by bypassing deliberation in anxious consumers — is worth confronting before scaling.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Buying from a virtual avatar can feel consequence-free because there is no one on the other side to judge your choices. That absence of social friction, the study suggests, is exactly what makes impulse purchases easier.
studies.caveats: Experimental stimuli and short-term behavioral intentions rather than observed purchases; the abstract does not report sample sizes, composition or country, and the influencer-type and realism manipulations were artificial exposures rather than ongoing follows.
studies.verdict_notes: Dual-pathway model, realism moderation and the product-risk boundary are reported accurately, and the digest correctly notes the abstract gives no sample details; the headline drops the appearance-anxiety precondition.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- Interface architecture keeps turning out to be a persuasion variable rather than a UX detail. "One 'swap and save' nudge can rewire a shopper's habit for 10 trips" (W4406862001) and "Clustering a few bad reviews together makes them feel like the majority" (W7224935301) extend the previous digest's "'Pick what you want' and 'reject what you don't' are not the same shopping task" (W7128495320) — all three locate the lever in how the flow asks the question, not in the merchandise.
- AI assistance remains conditional on what is being bought. "Typing beats talking: text AI recommendations get adopted more than voice" (W7223653038) splits on search versus experience goods, directly paralleling "Let AI pick your vacation, not your phone" (W7220380523), which split on experiential versus material purchases. Two different AI design decisions, the same category boundary.
- Sustainability and quality badges are still non-portable, context-dependent levers. "Sustainability labels moved shoppers on flour — and did nothing for shoes" (W7222938044) and "Japanese shoppers trust 'made here' far more than they trust awards" (W7225201218) echo "Shoppers trust the logo and the claim for different reasons" (W7215077900) and "Latin American coffee drinkers will pay extra for organic and fair trade" (W7214722003): the plain, concrete claim outperforms the prestige or socially framed one, and credibility does not travel across categories.
- Gender-blind consumer models continue to fail. "Body-positive ads land with women — and backfire with men" (W7224022072) and the stronger female association in "Lonely shoppers aren't just buying more, they're buying impulsively" (W7225196252) join the previous digest's "The standard model of healthy eating was built on mostly female samples" (W7214384564).
- Non-human brand agents remain an active thread. "Shoppers let their guard down with AI influencers" (W7224077478) and "Instagram commenters are running their own forensic audits of AI influencers" (W7225171472) continue the line running through "A dog eating the snack makes shoppers think it's healthier" (W7220383982) and "'I'm still waiting in your cart'" (W7220393204) — but with a sharper edge, since the mechanism here is the absence of social judgment rather than added warmth.

**Advances**
- The interface thread finally gets field evidence. The standing gap after W7128495320 and the previous run's scroll/returns work was observed behavior rather than lab tasks; "One 'swap and save' nudge" (W4406862001) supplies longitudinal platform data showing a single prompt resetting repurchase defaults for roughly ten trips.
- State-dependent demand broadens from nostalgia to loneliness. "The more jobs you juggle, the more you crave nostalgia" (W7220388832) framed consumption as a self-continuity repair; "Lonely shoppers reach for busier packaging" (W7221515577) and "Lonely shoppers aren't just buying more" (W7225196252) add a second emotional state with its own mechanisms — symbolic security and impulse dysregulation.
- Platform trust-signal integrity moves from seller identity to audience response. "'Service camouflage'" (W7215041317) documented how operators sever reviews from the business; "Instagram commenters are running their own forensic audits" (W7225171472) shows audiences building collective countermeasures in public, and "Clustering a few bad reviews" (W7224935301) shows how fragile the signal is even when honest.

**Counterpoints**
- The established "visual maximalism underperforms" finding — AR vividness adding nothing (W7219780211), redundant photo galleries suppressing bookings (W7213493969), faces cutting views (W7212428236) — meets two findings that reward complexity. "Cool colors can excite too — if you use more than one" (W7223786954) and "Lonely shoppers reach for busier packaging" (W7221515577) both show visual complexity working, via curiosity and via symbolic security. The reconcilable distinction is fidelity versus complexity, and it needs testing.
- The unresolved FOMO/JOMO tension from last run tips further. "In livestream selling, chatting with viewers outsells the hard hook" (W7225239935) finds urgency-led hooks weakest for high-involvement symbolic products, siding with "Advertising the joy of missing out" (W7214744519) against the FOMO amplification seen in "Why people go out at night" (W7203639635).

**New themes**
- Competitive strategy as an explanation for sameness: "Why rival products end up nearly identical" (W7222569592) has no counterpart in the previous digest.
- Macroeconomic perception as a demand driver: "The more unequal people think their society is, the more they buy self-improvement" (W7224997542).
- Household money mechanics: "People who check receipts, not memory, weather financial shocks better" (W7225263524).
- Marketing-claim ethics and denominator framing: "Business schools say AACSB accreditation puts them in the top 5%" (W7225152811).
- Emotion-specific crisis damage measured with eye tracking: "Eye tracking shows bad brand news wins the attention battle" (W7223841933).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Several studies in this batch converge on emotional state — not demographics, not stated preference — as the variable that actually predicts what people buy and how badly. Loneliness drives impulsive and compulsive purchasing through a self-regulation failure at checkout (W7225196252) and pushes the same shoppers toward densely designed, "protective" packaging (W7221515577); appearance anxiety converts into impulse buying specifically when the seller is an AI avatar with no capacity to judge you (W7224077478); perceived inequality raises demand for self-improvement products through status ambition (W7224997542); and status-motivated experience purchases leave buyers with frustrated psychological needs rather than the promised well-being (W7224107456). Taken together, the batch describes commercial formats that perform best precisely when the buyer is least equipped to deliberate.

**Why pitch this now:** Regulators are actively writing rules on dark patterns and vulnerable consumers while brands scale exactly the formats these studies implicate — synthetic influencers, livestream selling, one-click checkout — and loneliness is simultaneously being treated as a public-health issue in several markets.

**Angle:** A reported feature on mood as the new segmentation variable: who can detect emotional state from behavioral signals, which formats monetize it, what the evidence does and does not show about harm, and where the line sits between resonance and exploitation. Written for brand, commerce and compliance leaders, with a consumer throughline about why your worst purchases cluster in your worst weeks.

**Potential headlines:**
- Loneliness is becoming a marketing segment
- The avatar sells more because nobody is judging you
- Why your worst purchases arrive in your worst weeks

**Potential outlets:**
- **Marketing Week** — its readers are already being asked to square inclusive and wellbeing positioning with conversion targets, and this is the evidence base for where that tension actually bites.
- **Digiday** — closest to the commerce formats implicated here (livestream shopping, AI influencers, checkout friction), and well placed to report how platforms are or aren't auditing them.
- **The Guardian (Money/Consumer)** — runs the loneliness-and-spending story for a general readership without needing a trade frame, and the expense-tracking evidence gives it a practical counterweight.
- **WIRED** — strong on persuasion technology and synthetic personas, and the "no social evaluation, so no brakes" mechanism is a genuinely new explanation for why AI sellers convert.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **One "swap and save" nudge can rewire a shopper's habit for 10 trips (Work ID W4406862001):** A single interface prompt breaks supermarket brand loyalty for roughly ten trips, and the stickiness comes from discovery rather than savings — a trial-generation weapon for challengers and a quiet threat to incumbents, for a retail trade explainer or an FMCG-marketing news brief.
- **Japanese shoppers trust "made here" far more than they trust awards (Work ID W7225201218):** Gold-medal badges may be doing almost nothing on their own, with origin claims carrying the work and regional cues paying off only where the place already has a good image, for a food and drink marketing trade piece or a packaging-design column.
- **Lonely shoppers aren't just buying more, they're buying impulsively (Work ID W7225196252):** Loneliness-driven overspending reframed as a speed problem at the point of purchase rather than deliberate retail therapy, with a direct implication for saved cards and countdown timers, for a personal-finance column or a consumer-psychology explainer.
- **Why rival products end up nearly identical (Work ID W7222569592):** Low ad spend in a crowded category may be a tacit truce rather than timidity — and it collapses the moment one firm spends aggressively, for a CMO-audience strategy column or a business-school-style explainer on competitive war-gaming.
- **Cool colors can excite too — if you use more than one (Work ID W7223786954):** Eight experiments with eye tracking and skin response break the red-equals-excitement design rule, giving tech, finance and sustainability brands a route to arousal without a warm palette, for a brand-design trade feature.
- **Clustering a few bad reviews together makes them feel like the majority (Work ID W7224935301):** "Most recent first" and infinite scroll can make three critics look like a consensus, with the effect stronger on mobile — a review-sorting audit for retail and platform teams, and a practical self-defense tip for shoppers, for an e-commerce trade explainer or a consumer-tech column.
- **Typing beats talking: text AI recommendations get adopted more than voice (Work ID W7223653038):** Modality is a persuasion variable, not an engineering choice: text for spec-heavy goods, voice for experiential buys and distracted shoppers, for a retail-technology trade piece or an AI-commerce column.
- **Eye tracking shows bad brand news wins the attention battle (Work ID W7223841933):** Crisis damage is surgical — contempt for worker-treatment failures, disgust for integrity failures — so generic positive content cannot repair the specific belief that was hit, for a PR and crisis-communications trade feature.
- **In livestream selling, chatting with viewers outsells the hard hook (Work ID W7225239935):** Hook-and-urgency coaching looks wrong for higher-ticket symbolic goods, where conversation builds the trust that converts, for a social-commerce trade brief or a creator-economy column.
- **Lonely shoppers reach for busier packaging (Work ID W7221515577):** A decade of minimalist orthodoxy challenged by evidence that emotional state, not design fashion, decides which pack wins — and that complex designs read as protective, for a packaging-design trade explainer or a general-interest piece on how mood shapes taste.
- **The more unequal people think their society is, the more they buy self-improvement (Work ID W7224997542):** The self-optimization boom traced to perceived reward gaps and status ambition rather than anxiety, which flips the positioning logic for courses, coaching and fitness, for a business-magazine column or a consumer-culture explainer.
- **"Buy experiences, not things" only works if you want them for the right reasons (Work ID W7224107456):** The happiness claim underpinning a decade of travel and events marketing holds only conditionally, and the harmful route — buying experiences out of image pressure — is the more reliable one, for a travel and hospitality trade piece or a general-interest wellbeing column.
- **Sustainability labels moved shoppers on flour — and did nothing for shoes (Work ID W7222938044):** Eco-cues land only where consumers already expect an origin story, and the community co-creation claim underperformed a plain environmental label — a budgeting question before any certification spend, for a sustainability-marketing trade explainer.
- **Business schools say AACSB accreditation puts them in the top 5% (Work ID W7225152811):** A technically true scarcity statistic that misleads a domestic audience, assessed against FTC and advertising-ethics standards — and coming from the institutions that teach marketing ethics, for an advertising-regulation news piece or a higher-education consumer column.
- **Body-positive ads land with women — and backfire with men (Work ID W7224022072):** Inclusive casting shows a gendered payoff, with large-size male models producing negative emotional response against muscular ideals — a creative-testing caution for menswear, fitness and grooming, for an advertising trade news item or a culture desk piece on male body ideals.
- **People who check receipts, not memory, weather financial shocks better (Work ID W7225263524):** Budgeting advice focuses on whether people budget; this says the capture method is what separates real budgeting from the illusion of it, for a personal-finance column or a fintech product-strategy brief.
- **Instagram commenters are running their own forensic audits of AI influencers (Work ID W7225171472):** AI disclosure appears to invite scrutiny rather than defuse it, and audiences are crowdsourcing authenticity checks in the comments — making the comment section part of the creative, for an influencer-marketing trade feature or a platform-culture piece.
- **Shoppers let their guard down with AI influencers — but only on low-stakes buys (Work ID W7224077478):** Virtual sellers appear to work by removing social judgment, which converts in fashion and beauty and fails in health and finance — an effectiveness finding and a consumer-protection problem in the same result, for a marketing-ethics column or a consumer-tech explainer.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Marketing Research Digest — Consumer Psychology — 2026-11-05
**Checked:** 2026-11-05 | **Studies reviewed:** 18
**Primary audience:** marketers and brand leaders | **Secondary audience:** general readers and consumers

---

### Study 1: One "swap and save" nudge can rewire a shopper's habit for 10 trips
**Work ID:** W4406862001 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Duration overstated as permanent** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "a single, cheap interface element can permanently break habitual brand loyalty in a repeat-purchase category"
- **Abstract says:** "shoppers who switched to an alternative product after receiving a prompt were 23.7 percentage points more likely to select that alternative product in subsequent visits, with this effect lasting for up to 10 shopping trips"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports an effect bounded at roughly 10 shopping trips; "permanently" contradicts both the abstract and the digest's own caveat about a short horizon.
- **Suggested fix:** "Replace "permanently break" with "disrupt for a run of about 10 subsequent trips"."

**Issue B. "Months" not supported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a single prompt is enough to reset the default for months"
- **Abstract says:** "with this effect lasting for up to 10 shopping trips"
- **Problem:** The abstract measures persistence in shopping trips, not calendar time; converting to "months" adds an unsupported time frame.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "for roughly ten subsequent shopping trips" instead of "for months"."

### Study 2: Japanese shoppers trust "made here" far more than they trust awards
**Work ID:** W7225201218 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Moderation stated too absolutely** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "it was associated with choice more positively only among consumers who rated the linked place as attractive"
- **Abstract says:** "Award recognition did not function as a uniformly positive signal; its conditional association with choice was more positive at higher levels of perceived Soma City attractiveness."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a continuous conditional association (more positive at higher attractiveness), not a threshold effect present "only" in one group.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "was more positively associated with choice the more attractive consumers rated the linked place"."

**Issue B. "Entirely" overstates dependence** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "can depend entirely on whether the consumer has a positive image of the place behind the product"
- **Abstract says:** "its conditional association with choice was more positive at higher levels of perceived Soma City attractiveness"
- **Problem:** "Entirely" implies the award signal has no standalone association, which the abstract does not establish.
- **Suggested fix:** "Soften to "appears to depend partly on whether the consumer has a positive image of the place"."

### Study 3: Lonely shoppers aren't just buying more, they're buying impulsively
**Work ID:** W7225196252 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 4: Why rival products end up nearly identical: advertising less is a way to compete less
**Work ID:** W7222569592 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 5: Cool colors can excite too — if you use more than one
**Work ID:** W7223786954 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 6: Clustering a few bad reviews together makes them feel like the majority
**Work ID:** W7224935301 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Unsupported magnitude wording** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "made consumers believe that viewpoint was far more common than it was ... scattering the same reviews among the majority weakened the effect substantially"
- **Abstract says:** "grouping minority reviews into a contiguous run increases their perceived prevalence and in turn shifts product evaluations accordingly, whereas scattered minority reviews have weaker effects"
- **Problem:** The abstract gives no effect sizes; "far more common" and "weakened substantially" imply quantified magnitudes that are not reported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "more common than it was" and "produced weaker effects" without the intensifiers."

### Study 7: Typing beats talking: text AI recommendations get adopted more than voice
**Work ID:** W7223653038 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Country attributed to all experiments** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "plus four controlled experiments in China"
- **Abstract says:** "Study 1 replicates the core modality effect in a controlled Chinese experiment."
- **Problem:** Only Study 1 is explicitly identified as Chinese; the locations of Studies 2–4 are not stated in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "plus four controlled experiments, at least one of which was run in China" or note the location is specified only for Study 1."

### Study 8: Eye tracking shows bad brand news wins the attention battle — and specific crises leave specific scars
**Work ID:** W7223841933 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Dropped moderator** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Anger and sadness did not mediate the damage, and the hit to the specific legitimacy belief was larger and more persistent than the hit to overall brand evaluation."
- **Abstract says:** "Anger and sadness did not mediate these relationships, while social identification strengthened both pathways."
- **Problem:** The abstract names social identification as a moderator that strengthened both emotional pathways; the digest omits it, losing a condition that matters for who is most affected.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add that consumers who identified more strongly with the brand showed stronger emotional pathways."

**Issue B. Sample composition asserted** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "these are controlled experiments with student-scale samples"
- **Abstract says:** "Study 1 uses within-participant eye tracking (n = 117). Study 2 combines eye tracking and survey measures in a randomised experiment (n = 285). Study 3 uses a three-wave longitudinal experiment (n = 279 at T3)."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not describe participants as students or state their composition; "student-scale" implies a sample type that cannot be verified.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "moderate sample sizes of undisclosed composition"."

**Issue C. "Permanently" overstates persistence** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "you may still think the brand is fine overall while permanently doubting that it treats its staff decently"
- **Abstract says:** "Legitimacy threats also produced larger, more persistent changes in the affected legitimacy belief than in overall brand evaluation."
- **Problem:** "More persistent" across three waves is not the same as permanent; the digest's own caveat notes the limited longitudinal horizon.
- **Suggested fix:** "Replace "permanently" with "more durably" or "still doubting weeks later"."

### Study 9: In livestream selling, chatting with viewers outsells the hard hook
**Work ID:** W7225239935 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 10: Lonely shoppers reach for busier packaging
**Work ID:** W7221515577 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Moderation described as disappearing** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The effect was strongest among people low in a dispositional sense of security and faded among those who already felt secure."
- **Abstract says:** "the positive effect of loneliness on the desire for symbolic security is stronger among consumers with lower levels of security trait and weaker among those with higher levels of security trait"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a weaker effect at high security trait, not an absent one; "faded" implies elimination.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change "faded" to "was weaker"."

### Study 11: The more unequal people think their society is, the more they buy self-improvement
**Work ID:** W7224997542 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline implies actual purchasing** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The more unequal people think their society is, the more they buy self-improvement"
- **Abstract says:** "high (vs. low) perceived economic inequality significantly increases consumers' preferences for self‐improvement (vs. non‐self‐improvement) products ... extends to more direct consumption‐related outcomes, including purchase intention and recommendation likelihood"
- **Problem:** The measured outcomes are stated preferences, purchase intention and recommendation likelihood, not observed buying; the headline reads as behavior. The body and caveats are careful, so this is a headline-only slip.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to something like "...the more they say they want self-improvement products" or "...the stronger their preference for self-improvement purchases"."

### Study 12: "Buy experiences, not things" only works if you want them for the right reasons
**Work ID:** W7224107456 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 13: Sustainability labels moved shoppers on flour — and did nothing for shoes
**Work ID:** W7222938044 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 14: Business schools say AACSB accreditation puts them in the top 5% — in the US it's more like half
**Work ID:** W7225152811 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 15: Body-positive ads land with women — and backfire with men
**Work ID:** W7224022072 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 16: People who check receipts, not memory, weather financial shocks better
**Work ID:** W7225263524 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal verb for an associational finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "using more sources — particularly financial records and receipts rather than memory — produced fewer imprecise and incomplete expense records"
- **Abstract says:** "Employing more sources is associated with higher tracking data quality (fewer imprecise and incomplete records), and consulting financial records and receipts outperforms memory."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports an association from cross-sectional survey and diary data; "produced" states causation. The caveat covers the tracking-quality-to-resilience link but not this one.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change "produced" to "was associated with"."

**Issue B. Headline chains two associations into one causal claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "People who check receipts, not memory, weather financial shocks better"
- **Abstract says:** "consulting financial records and receipts outperforms memory. We further find that greater precision in recorded amounts is associated with stronger household financial resilience"
- **Problem:** Receipt use is linked to record precision, and precision is separately linked to resilience; the abstract does not test a direct receipts-to-resilience effect, and neither link is causal.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe as "Precise expense records go with better resilience — and precision comes from receipts, not recall"."

### Study 17: Instagram commenters are running their own forensic audits of AI influencers
**Work ID:** W7225171472 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 18: Shoppers let their guard down with AI influencers — but only on low-stakes buys
**Work ID:** W7224077478 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline generalizes a conditional effect to shoppers at large** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Shoppers let their guard down with AI influencers — but only on low-stakes buys"
- **Abstract says:** "a dual pathway model in which appearance anxiety drives consumption through a fear of missing out (FOMO)-mediated compensatory route ... and a direct disinhibitory route unique to AI contexts"
- **Problem:** The disinhibition route is modelled as a pathway from appearance anxiety, not a general effect on all shoppers; the headline reads as universal. The body text does specify appearance anxiety.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add the precondition, e.g. "Appearance-anxious shoppers let their guard down with AI influencers — but only on low-stakes buys"."

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | One "swap and save" nudge can rewire a shopper's habit for 10 trips | ⚠️ Minor issues | Core numbers (23.7pp, 10 trips, discovery mechanism) are accurate, but "permanently" and "for months" in the framing overstate a 10-trip horizon the digest's own caveat flags as short. |
| 2 | Japanese shoppers trust "made here" far more than they trust awards | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, N, observation count and main effects all match; the award moderation is described slightly more absolutely than the abstract's conditional wording. |
| 3 | Lonely shoppers aren't just buying more, they're buying impulsively | ✅ Accurate | Sample sizes, indirect effect (0.140), gender patterns and the exploratory status of the neural pathway all match the abstract; caveats are appropriately cautious. |
| 4 | Why rival products end up nearly identical: advertising less is a way to compete less | ✅ Accurate | Faithful summary of an analytical modeling paper, with the theoretical nature and the travel-cost assumption dependence both flagged. |
| 5 | Cool colors can excite too — if you use more than one | ✅ Accurate | Experiment count, preregistration, N=1,724, biometric measures, real-choice studies, curiosity mechanism and WTP/choice outcomes all match. (Abstract notes only six of the eight experiments appear in the main text, a detail the digest omits without distorting the finding.) |
| 6 | Clustering a few bad reviews together makes them feel like the majority | ⚠️ Minor issues | All four experiments, the mediator, and all three boundary conditions (cognitive load, mobile vs desktop, positive and negative minorities) are correctly reported; only the magnitude intensifiers go beyond the abstract. |
| 7 | Typing beats talking: text AI recommendations get adopted more than voice | ⚠️ Minor issues | Five studies, the field component, the search/experience moderation, processing fluency mediation and the multitasking reversal are all accurate; the claim that all four experiments ran in China goes slightly beyond the abstract. |
| 8 | Eye tracking shows bad brand news wins the attention battle — and specific crises leave specific scars | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample sizes and the emotion-specific pathways are reported correctly, but the social identification moderator is dropped, the samples are described as "student-scale" without support, and "permanently" overstates persistence. |
| 9 | In livestream selling, chatting with viewers outsells the hard hook | ✅ Accurate | N=603, three speech conditions, the ranking of effects, the high-involvement symbolic product context and the emotion→trust→intention mediation all match; caveats correctly note stated intention rather than purchases. |
| 10 | Lonely shoppers reach for busier packaging | ⚠️ Minor issues | Seven studies, N=1,636, the complex-packaging effect and the symbolic security mechanism are accurate; the security-trait moderation is described as the effect "fading" rather than weakening. |
| 11 | The more unequal people think their society is, the more they buy self-improvement | ⚠️ Minor issues | Study count, countries, N, mediator and null alternative mechanisms all match; headline converts preference/intention into purchase behavior. |
| 12 | "Buy experiences, not things" only works if you want them for the right reasons | ✅ Accurate | Sample (1,409 collected, 1,324 retained), country groupings, and the asymmetry between the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways are reported correctly; caveats flag the cross-sectional design. |
| 13 | Sustainability labels moved shoppers on flour — and did nothing for shoes | ✅ Accurate | N=991 Brazilian online survey experiment, three cues, two categories, strongest effect for the environmental/sustainability label, null results for shoes and null moderation by knowledge and values all match the abstract; caveats correctly note intention rather than purchase. |
| 14 | Business schools say AACSB accreditation puts them in the top 5% — in the US it's more like half | ✅ Accurate | The ~52% US figure, the 5–6% global claim, the four cited ethics codes, and the descriptive/normative nature of the paper are all consistent with the abstract. |
| 15 | Body-positive ads land with women — and backfire with men | ✅ Accurate | Direction of both effects and the distinct positive/negative emotion mediators match; the digest correctly flags that the abstract reports no sample size, composition or country. |
| 16 | People who check receipts, not memory, weather financial shocks better | ⚠️ Minor issues | Data source, 65% figure and the two associations are reported correctly, but the body uses a causal verb and the headline chains two separate associations. |
| 17 | Instagram commenters are running their own forensic audits of AI influencers | ✅ Accurate | Comment count, post count, accounts, date range, double coding, and the 100/128 vs 32 thread split with their respective conditions all match; caveats correctly frame it as content analysis of discourse. |
| 18 | Shoppers let their guard down with AI influencers — but only on low-stakes buys | ⚠️ Minor issues | Dual-pathway model, realism moderation and the product-risk boundary are reported accurately, and the digest correctly notes the abstract gives no sample details; the headline drops the appearance-anxiety precondition. |

**Total issues:** 14 (12 Minor, 2 Moderate, 0 Major)
